# Godstack: complete public documentation

Single-header C libraries for platform services, graphics, UI, text, and developer tools. Use only the headers your application needs.

Source: https://github.com/godxgun/godstack
License: MIT (https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/license/)

This file includes only the public documentation corpus used for the site's catalog, search, and Markdown outputs. It does not include private repository files or a runtime backend. Page boundaries and source URLs are provided below.


---

<!-- BEGIN PAGE: /godstack/ai/ -->
# AI and agent documentation

Documentation: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/ai/
Markdown: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/ai.md
Description: Public machine-readable Godstack documentation endpoints and grounded guidance for coding agents.


Godstack publishes documentation formats that coding assistants and other automated readers can fetch. These are static documentation resources, not an execution or tool backend:

- [llms.txt](/godstack/llms.txt) is a compact index for discovering site content.
- [llms-small.txt](/godstack/llms-small.txt) and [llms-full.txt](/godstack/llms-full.txt) provide different-sized text collections.
- [catalog.json](/godstack/catalog.json) is a machine-readable content catalog.
- Individual documentation pages have Markdown output, for example [Cast Markdown](/godstack/docs/cast.md) and [Getting started Markdown](/godstack/guides/getting-started.md).
- Agent guidance is available as [SKILL.md](/godstack/agent/SKILL.md) and [AGENTS.md](/godstack/agent/AGENTS.md).

These are explicit URLs to fetch or link from your project; do not assume an editor discovers or loads them automatically. Availability and exact formats depend on the deployed site. There is no MCP server or backend currently available. A possible future MCP adapter could expose catalog search and documentation retrieval, but it does not exist today.

## Add documentation to a coding workflow

### Codex

Fetch [llms-small.txt](/godstack/llms-small.txt) and the relevant page's Markdown (for example [Grit](/godstack/docs/grit.md)) into the repository, then link the local paths from `AGENTS.md` or a relevant nested `AGENTS.md`. Codex reads repository guidance files; it does not automatically discover this website's resources.

```text
In this repository, first read the local Godstack documentation index and the relevant library's Markdown page, then inspect the corresponding header and demo. Treat the header as the API source of truth. Keep the implementation macro in exactly one translation unit where required, respect documented limitations and ownership, and do not assume APIs from another library. If no local docs are present, fetch `/llms-small.txt` and the relevant `/docs/<library>.md` explicitly from this site's origin. Verify examples by compiling when feasible.
```

### Claude Code

Fetch [llms-small.txt](/godstack/llms-small.txt) and the relevant Markdown page, then place their paths and reading instructions in a project guidance file such as `CLAUDE.md` (or the applicable Claude Code project instructions). This file is optional project guidance; a URL alone does not make Claude fetch it.

```text
Before using a Godstack library, read the project-linked llms-small.txt and the relevant per-page Markdown, then inspect the corresponding C header and demo. Follow only documented APIs and limitations; preserve ownership/lifetime requirements and put any implementation macro in one translation unit. Fetch `/llms-small.txt` and the relevant `/docs/<library>.md` explicitly from this site's origin if local documentation is unavailable. Compile examples when feasible.
```

### Cursor

Fetch [llms-small.txt](/godstack/llms-small.txt) and the relevant Markdown page into project files and add them to Cursor's project context or reference them in project rules. Cursor does not automatically load these site URLs merely because this page mentions them.

```text
Use the project-provided Godstack llms-small.txt and relevant library Markdown page as discovery aids, then verify APIs against the actual header and demo. Respect the header's version, constraints, and ownership rules. Do not infer unsupported symbols or platform support. If the project has no local docs, explicitly fetch `/llms-small.txt` and `/docs/<library>.md` from this site's origin before coding; compile examples where feasible.
```

# Cast

Documentation: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/cast/
Markdown: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/cast.md
Description: A practical guide to tokenizing and walking C source with caller-owned memory.


# Cast

Cast (C AST) reads C source from memory and gives you its tokens and a tree of its file-scope
declarations: variables, function prototypes and definitions, their types, pointers, arrays and
parameters. It is meant for tools that need to look at C code, such as binding generators,
documentation tools and template compilers. It does not load files, does not allocate, and skips
preprocessor lines instead of expanding them.

Define `CAST_IMPLEMENTATION` in exactly one translation unit before including `Cast.h`. Other
translation units include the header without it.

## Tokenizing Source

The first thing to try is splitting a line of C into tokens:

```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#define CAST_IMPLEMENTATION
#include "Cast.h"

int main(void)
{
    unsigned char storage[4096];
    char source[] = "int answer;";
    CastMemory memory = cast_memory_create(storage, sizeof storage);
    size_t count = 0;
    CastToken *tokens = cast_tokenize(&memory, source, strlen(source), &count);
    if (!tokens) return 1;
    printf("tokens: %zu\n", count);
    return 0;
}
```

This prints `tokens: 3`. `cast_memory_create()` turns your buffer into an arena; every token,
node and name Cast produces is stored in it. `cast_tokenize()` returns an array of `count` tokens,
or NULL when the input is empty or the arena is too small.

Tokens do not copy text. Each `CastToken` has a `type` and the byte offset (`arg`) and length
(`arglen`) of its text in the source, so keep the source alive and unchanged while you use the
results. Comments and lines starting with `#` are skipped; macros are not expanded.

## Reading Tokens

`cast_token_type()` names a token type: `IDENT`, `KW` (keyword), `NUMBER`, `STRING`, `CHAR`,
`PUNCT` or `ERROR`. Print the text through the offset and length:

```c
for (size_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
    CastToken t = tokens[i];
    printf("%-6s %.*s\n", cast_token_type(t.type), t.arglen, source + t.arg);
}
```

For `int answer;` this prints:

```text
KW     int
IDENT  answer
PUNCT  ;
```

An unterminated string or a character C does not use comes back as an `ERROR` token instead of
stopping the tokenizer.

## Parsing Declarations

`cast_ast()` parses the tokens into a tree. Node 0 is the translation unit (`"tu"`); its children
are the file-scope declarations in source order. Walk the tree with `first_child` and
`next_sibling`; an index of zero ends a list, since the root is never anyone's child:

```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#define CAST_IMPLEMENTATION
#include "Cast.h"

static void describe(CastAst *ast, CastNode node)
{
    const char *type = "?";
    int stars = 0, arrays = 0;
    for (size_t i = node.first_child; i; i = cast_ast_node(ast, i).next_sibling) {
        CastNode child = cast_ast_node(ast, i);
        if (strcmp(child.msg, "type") == 0) type = child.name;
        else if (strcmp(child.msg, "ptr") == 0) stars++;
        else if (strcmp(child.msg, "array") == 0) arrays++;
    }
    printf("%s", type);
    if (stars || node.name)
        printf(" %.*s%s", stars, "********", node.name ? node.name : "");
    while (arrays--) printf("[]");
}

int main(void)
{
    static unsigned char storage[64 * 1024];
    char source[] =
        "#include <stdio.h>\n"
        "static const char *lookup(int id, char **out);\n"
        "int counts[16], total;\n"
        "void reset(void) { total = 0; }\n";

    CastMemory memory = cast_memory_create(storage, sizeof storage);
    size_t token_count = 0, node_count = 0;
    CastToken *tokens = cast_tokenize(&memory, source, strlen(source), &token_count);
    if (!tokens) return 1;
    CastAst *ast = cast_ast(&memory, tokens, token_count, &node_count);
    if (!ast) return 1;

    CastNode root = cast_ast_node(ast, 0);
    for (size_t i = root.first_child; i; i = cast_ast_node(ast, i).next_sibling) {
        CastNode decl = cast_ast_node(ast, i);
        printf("line %u: %-4s ", (unsigned)decl.line, decl.msg);
        describe(ast, decl);
        if (strcmp(decl.msg, "func") == 0) {
            const char *separator = "";
            printf("(");
            for (size_t p = decl.first_child; p; p = cast_ast_node(ast, p).next_sibling) {
                CastNode param = cast_ast_node(ast, p);
                if (strcmp(param.msg, "param") != 0) continue;
                printf("%s", separator);
                describe(ast, param);
                separator = ", ";
            }
            printf(")");
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```

It prints:

```text
line 2: func static const char *lookup(int id, char **out)
line 3: decl int counts[]
line 3: decl int total
line 4: func void reset(void)
```

Each node has a `msg` naming its kind: `"decl"` for variables, `"func"` for functions (prototype
or definition), `"param"` for parameters, `"type"` for the specifier text (its `name` keeps
storage classes and qualifiers, such as `static const char`), `"ptr"` for each `*`, and `"array"`
for each `[...]`. `name` is the declared identifier and `line` its source line; `arg` and
`arglen` locate the identifier in the source. Function bodies, initializers and `struct` member
lists are skipped, so they produce no nodes.

Names are copied into the arena, but `arg` offsets still refer to the source. `cast_ast()` reads
the source recorded by the most recent `cast_tokenize()` on the same memory, so tokenize and parse
one input before starting the next.

## Handling Unparsable Input

Cast does not stop at the first problem. When a file-scope item does not start with a type, Cast
adds an `"error"` node whose `name` is the offending token, skips to the next `;`, and carries on:

```c
char source[] = "int ok;\nreturn 0;\nfloat also_ok;\n";
/* tu children: decl ok, error "return" (line 2), decl also_ok */
```

Report error nodes with their `line` instead of treating them as declarations. Because
preprocessor lines are skipped, a declaration produced by a macro is invisible to Cast, and an
identifier type such as `size_t` is recognized only from context (an identifier followed by
another identifier or `*`).

## Sizing and Reusing Memory

Tokens take `sizeof(CastToken)` bytes each, and `cast_ast()` reserves room for four nodes per
token plus the declared names. A buffer of a few hundred bytes per token is ample. When either
call returns NULL for non-empty input, give it a larger buffer.

`cast_memory_clear()` empties the arena without freeing anything, so the same buffer can parse the
next input. Everything returned before the clear becomes invalid. Cool's template transpiler,
`CoolTranspiler.c`, uses Cast this way to read each template's parameter list.

See [Cast symbols](/godstack/symbols/cast/) for the generated declarations.


<!-- END PAGE: /godstack/docs/cast/ -->

# Cool

Documentation: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/cool/
Markdown: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/cool.md
Description: Use Cool output helpers for escaped text, trusted markup, and a limited Markdown subset.


# Cool

Cool generates HTML from C. It writes straight to a `FILE *` stream: escaped text, raw markup,
and a small Markdown subset. A separate transpiler turns `.cool` template files into plain C
functions that call the same helpers. Cool does not allocate, buffer or sanitize markup for you.

Define `COOL_IMPLEMENTATION` in exactly one translation unit before including `Cool.h`. Other
translation units include the header without it.

## Writing Text

The first thing to try is writing user text into a page. `cool_html_txt()` escapes `<`, `>` and
`&` and writes the result to standard output:

```c
#define COOL_IMPLEMENTATION
#include "Cool.h"

int main(void)
{
    cool_html_txt("Hello & welcome", 15);
    return 0;
}
```

This prints `Hello &amp; welcome`. The length is in bytes; output also stops at the first NUL.
`cool_html_txt()` is meant for element content. It does not escape quotes, so it is not safe for
untrusted values placed inside attribute values.

## Writing Markup

Markup you control is written unescaped. `COOL_SV()` wraps a string literal with its length;
`cool_html_raw_cstr()` takes any pointer and length; `cool_htmlf_raw()` is `printf` into the
stream. None of the raw helpers escape anything, so use them for literals and numbers, and send
every user-supplied string through `cool_html_txt()`.

```c
static const char *const names[] = {"Peak", "Rend", "Fuse <beta>"};

cool_html_raw(COOL_SV("<ul class=\"libs\">\n"));
for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
    cool_htmlf_raw("  <li data-index=\"%d\">", i);
    cool_html_txt(names[i], strlen(names[i]));
    cool_html_raw(COOL_SV("</li>\n"));
}
cool_html_raw(COOL_SV("</ul>\n"));
```

The third name is written as `Fuse &lt;beta&gt;`.

## Choosing the Output Stream

Output goes to `COOL_OUTPUT`, which defaults to `stdout`. Define it before including the header.
It is evaluated on every write, so it can name a variable that you change at runtime. On POSIX
systems, `open_memstream()` captures a page in memory, ready to send as a response body:

```c
#define _POSIX_C_SOURCE 200809L
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

static FILE *cool_out;
#define COOL_OUTPUT cool_out
#define COOL_IMPLEMENTATION
#include "Cool.h"

int main(void)
{
    char *page = NULL;
    size_t size = 0;

    cool_out = open_memstream(&page, &size);
    if (!cool_out) return 1;
    cool_html_raw(COOL_SV("<h1>"));
    cool_html_txt("Status", 6);
    cool_html_raw(COOL_SV("</h1>\n"));
    fclose(cool_out); /* page and size are valid after the stream is closed */

    fwrite(page, 1, size, stdout);
    free(page);
    return 0;
}
```

The repository's doc generator uses this pattern to answer [Wire](/godstack/docs/wire/) requests.

## Rendering Markdown

`cool_md()` converts a Markdown subset to HTML and writes it to the same stream:

```c
static const char notes[] =
    "## Release\n"
    "\n"
    "The build is **ready**. See [the guide](/docs/cool/).\n"
    "\n"
    "- `cool_md` writes HTML\n"
    "- text is *escaped*\n"
    "\n"
    "| Library | Status |\n"
    "| ------- | ------ |\n"
    "| Cool    | ok     |\n";

cool_md(notes, sizeof notes - 1);
```

The supported subset is ATX headings (`#` to `######`), paragraphs, `-`/`*`/`+` bullet lists,
`1.` ordered lists, `---` rules, fenced code blocks (a simple language name becomes
`class="language-..."`), pipe tables, inline code, `**strong**`, `*emphasis*` and
`[text](url)` links. Nested lists, block quotes, images, setext headings and underscore emphasis
are not recognized; such lines come out as paragraph text.

Text and code are escaped, so HTML embedded in the Markdown is displayed rather than interpreted.
Link targets are escaped for the attribute, but their scheme is not checked: a `javascript:` URL
passes through. Filter links yourself when the Markdown comes from users.

## Compiling Templates

For larger pages, write markup in a `.cool` file and let `CoolTranspiler.c` turn each template
into a C function. A template starts with a line beginning with `COOL` followed by a C function
header, and ends with a line containing only `}`:

```html
COOL void LibCard(char *name, int version) {
    <div class="card">
        <h3>{ name }</h3>
        <span>v{ version }</span>
    </div>
}
```

Inside a template, `{ name }` inserts a parameter. `char *` parameters are written with
`cool_html_txt()`; numeric parameters go through `cool_htmlf_raw()` with a matching format.
An expression that is not exactly a parameter name is a transpile error. `@Func(args)` emits a
call to another C function, such as another template. Lines outside templates are copied to the
output unchanged.

Build the transpiler once, then generate C from the template:

```sh
cc -std=c99 -Wall -Wextra -I. CoolTranspiler.c -o cool_transpiler
./cool_transpiler view.cool -o view.cool.c
```

The generated file is a set of plain functions. Include it after `Cool.h` and `<string.h>`,
since text parameters are measured with `strlen()`:

```c
#include <string.h>
#define COOL_IMPLEMENTATION
#include "Cool.h"
#include "view.cool.c"

int main(void)
{
    LibCard("Cool", 1);
    return 0;
}
```

Parameters are escaped as element text, not as attribute values, so do not place untrusted
strings inside quoted attributes in a template. See
[`demos/doc-generator/`](https://github.com/godxgun/godstack/tree/main/demos/doc-generator) for a
template, its generated C, and a server that renders it.

See [Cool symbols](/godstack/symbols/cool/) for the generated declarations.


<!-- END PAGE: /godstack/docs/cool/ -->

# Fuse

Documentation: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/fuse/
Markdown: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/fuse.md
Description: Set up caller-backed canvas storage, feed input, and render Fuse commands.


# Fuse

Fuse is an immediate-mode UI library. Each frame you describe the interface with function calls
(divs, buttons, sliders, text boxes) and Fuse lays it out, handles pointer and keyboard input,
and returns a flat list of draw commands: rectangles, lines, triangles, clip regions, images and
text runs. It does not open windows or draw pixels; your renderer consumes the commands.

All state lives in one caller-provided buffer. Fuse does not allocate. Define
`FUSE_IMPLEMENTATION` in exactly one translation unit before including `Fuse.h`, compile as C99
or later, and link with `-lm`.

## Building a Frame

The first thing to try is a button that reports a click. This program runs headless: it feeds
three frames of pointer input, as a window's event loop would, and prints what happened:

```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#define FUSE_IMPLEMENTATION
#include "Fuse.h"

static bool frame(FuseCanvas ui, FusePointerState pointer, float x, float y)
{
    static char label[] = "Apply";
    size_t count = 0;

    fuse_canvas_pointer(ui, pointer, x, y);
    fuse_canvas_clear(ui);

    fuse_id(ui, "apply");
    bool clicked = fuse_button_text(ui, label, 20, 20, 120, 36,
                                    0xFF3A6EA5u, 0xFF5A8EC5u);

    FuseCmd *commands = fuse_canvas_draw(ui, &count);
    if (!commands) {
        fprintf(stderr, "fuse error %d\n", (int)fuse_canvas_error(ui));
        return false;
    }
    printf("%zu commands, first is a %.0fx%.0f rectangle\n",
           count, commands[0].rect.w, commands[0].rect.h);
    return clicked;
}

int main(void)
{
    FuseParams params = {.max_elements = 256, .max_windows = 1, .max_scopes = 16};
    size_t bytes = fuse_memory(&params);
    void *memory = malloc(bytes);
    if (!memory) return 1;

    FuseCanvas ui = fuse_place_in_memory(memory, bytes, &params);
    if (!ui) {
        free(memory);
        return 1;
    }
    fuse_canvas_resize(ui, 320, 200);

    frame(ui, FUSE_POINTER_NONE, 60, 40);       /* pointer moves over the button */
    frame(ui, FUSE_POINTER_PRESSED, 60, 40);    /* button pressed */
    if (frame(ui, FUSE_POINTER_RELEASED, 60, 40))
        printf("Apply clicked\n");

    free(memory);
    return 0;
}
```

`FuseParams` sets fixed capacities: `max_elements` counts every element built in a frame,
including the implicit root and each run of a text label; `max_scopes` bounds how deeply divs
nest; `max_windows` bounds docking windows. `fuse_memory()` returns the bytes needed and
`fuse_place_in_memory()` places the canvas in your buffer, which must be 8-byte aligned and stay
alive while the canvas is used. There is nothing to destroy: free the buffer when you are done.

Every frame follows the same order: report input (`fuse_canvas_pointer()`, plus wheel, text and
keys), call `fuse_canvas_clear()`, build the interface, then call `fuse_canvas_draw()`. Widgets
answer input using the boxes laid out in the previous frame, which is why the click arrives on
the frame where the pointer is released over the button. The returned commands live in the
canvas buffer until the next clear.

## Drawing the Commands

Each `FuseCmd` has a `type` and a matching union member. Coordinates are canvas pixels and colors
are `0xAARRGGBB`. Draw the commands in order; `z` is the layer set with `fuse_canvas_layer()`, if
you want to sort by it:

```c
size_t count = 0;
FuseCmd *commands = fuse_canvas_draw(ui, &count);
for (size_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
    const FuseCmd *c = &commands[i];
    switch (c->type) {
    case FUSE_CMD_RECT:       fill_rect(c->rect.x, c->rect.y, c->rect.w, c->rect.h, c->rect.color); break;
    case FUSE_CMD_LINE:       draw_line(&c->line); break;
    case FUSE_CMD_TRIANGLE:   fill_triangle(&c->triangle); break;
    case FUSE_CMD_CLIP_START: push_clip(c->clip.x, c->clip.y, c->clip.w, c->clip.h); break;
    case FUSE_CMD_CLIP_END:   pop_clip(); break;
    case FUSE_CMD_IMAGE:      draw_image(c->image.handle, c->image.x, c->image.y, c->image.w, c->image.h); break;
    case FUSE_CMD_TEXT:       draw_text_run(&c->text); break;
    }
}
```

The drawing functions are your renderer's. Clip commands nest; intersect each new clip with the
current one. `FUSE_CMD_IMAGE` carries the handle you passed to `fuse_image()`; Fuse never sees the
pixels. `FUSE_CMD_TEXT` comes from text boxes: `c->text.slot` indexes the `FuseFieldRun` array
returned by `fuse_canvas_fields()`, which holds the string, size, color and caret position for a
proportional font.

`FuseRend.h` is an optional adapter that tessellates these commands for [Rend](/godstack/docs/rend/) and
draws text with [Type](/godstack/docs/type/). It has its own implementation macro,
`FUSE_REND_IMPLEMENTATION`.

## Laying Out with Classes

A div is a rectangle that contains other elements. Without a class, children are placed at the
coordinates you pass, relative to the div. With a `FuseClass`, the div arranges its children in a
row or column, with padding and gaps, and the coordinates you pass are ignored:

```c
static const FuseClass toolbar = {
    .color = 0xFF202830u,
    .direction = FUSE_DIRECTION_ROW,
    .gap = 8,
    .pad_l = 8, .pad_r = 8, .pad_t = 6, .pad_b = 6,
    .align_y = FUSE_ALIGN_CENTER,
};
static char open_label[] = "Open", save_label[] = "Save", quit_label[] = "Quit";

fuse_div_begin(ui, 0, 0, 640, 48, &toolbar);
    fuse_id(ui, "open");
    bool open = fuse_button_text(ui, open_label, 0, 0, 80, 32, 0xFF405060u, 0xFF607080u);
    fuse_id(ui, "save");
    bool save = fuse_button_text(ui, save_label, 0, 0, 80, 32, 0xFF405060u, 0xFF607080u);
    fuse_space(ui);   /* takes the leftover width */
    fuse_id(ui, "quit");
    bool quit = fuse_button_text(ui, quit_label, 0, 0, 80, 32, 0xFF804040u, 0xFFA06060u);
fuse_div_end(ui);
```

A class's `width_sizing` and `height_sizing` decide how children are sized on each axis:
`FUSE_SIZING_FIT` keeps the size you passed, `FUSE_SIZING_FIXED` uses the class's `width` or
`height` in pixels, `FUSE_SIZING_PERCENT` uses them as a fraction of the div's inner size, and
`FUSE_SIZING_GROW` shares the leftover space. `fuse_sizing()` overrides the mode for the next
element only. `min_*` and `max_*` clamp the results; `color` paints the div's background (zero
means none).

For side-by-side columns, `fuse_col_begin()` splits a width by ratios. Build the first column,
call `fuse_col_switch()` for each next column, and finish with `fuse_col_end()`; the row takes the
height of its tallest column:

```c
static const float split[] = {0.3f, 0.7f};
static const FuseClass stack = {.direction = FUSE_DIRECTION_COLUMN, .gap = 4};

fuse_col_begin(ui, 0, 48, 640, &stack, split, 2);
    fuse_text(ui, 0, 0, 2, "Layers", 0xFFFFFFFFu);
    fuse_col_switch(ui);
    fuse_text(ui, 0, 0, 2, "Preview", 0xFFFFFFFFu);
fuse_col_end(ui);
```

`fuse_text()` draws the built-in 5x7 bitmap font, upper case only, scaled by an integer factor.
Each lit run of pixels becomes a rectangle command, so it needs no font or texture.

## Identifying Widgets

Every element gets an ID. Without `fuse_id()`, the ID comes from the parent and the element's
position among its siblings, so it changes when the tree above it changes shape. Call
`fuse_id(ui, "name")` (or `fuse_idi(ui, "row", i)` in loops) before any widget whose interaction
must survive such changes. Using the same ID twice in one frame fails the frame with
`FUSE_ERR_DUPLICATE_ID`.

Names are global to the canvas by default. After opening a named div, `fuse_div_scope()` makes the
names of its children local to it, so two panels can each contain a button called `"ok"`.
`fuse_element_is_hovered()` asks about a named element in the current scope.

## Sliders, Scrolling and Text Input

Widgets keep no values themselves; they read and write your variables:

```c
static float volume = 0.5f, scroll = 0.0f;
static char name[64] = "";
static int caret = -1;
static const FuseClass list = {.direction = FUSE_DIRECTION_COLUMN, .gap = 2};

fuse_id(ui, "volume");
fuse_slider(ui, 20, 80, 200, 16, 0xFF303A44u, 0xFFE0E0E0u, &volume);

fuse_id(ui, "list");
fuse_div_begin_scroll(ui, 20, 110, 200, 120, &list, &scroll);
for (int i = 0; i < 40; ++i)
    fuse_rect(ui, 0, 0, 200, 18, i % 2 ? 0xFF2A2A2Au : 0xFF333333u);
fuse_div_end(ui);

fuse_id(ui, "name");
if (fuse_textbox(ui, 240, 80, 200, 28, 6, 6, name, sizeof name, &caret,
                 "Your name", 16, 0xFF1E1E1Eu, 0xFF262626u, 0xFFFFFFFFu, 0xFF808080u,
                 1, NULL, NULL)) {
    /* name changed this frame */
}
```

The slider keeps its knob position in `0..1` and follows the pointer while it is held. A
scrolling div clips its children and stores its offset in `scroll`; feed wheel motion with
`fuse_canvas_wheel()` before building. A text box is focused by clicking it (or with
`fuse_focus()`); pass typed UTF-8 with `fuse_canvas_text()` and editing keys such as
`FUSE_KEY_BACKSPACE` with `fuse_canvas_key()`. The box edits `name` in place, keeps the
terminating NUL within `sizeof name`, and returns `true` when the text changed. By default it
accepts bytes 32 to 126; pass an `allow` callback to change that.

Other building blocks: `fuse_rect()` and `fuse_image()` place plain boxes,
`fuse_radial()` draws a ring menu and returns the hovered slice, and
`fuse_canvas_input_enabled()` turns off pointer handling for the widgets that follow, for
example behind a modal panel.

## Docking Windows

The docking API arranges named panels in tabs and splits that the user can drag, resize and
float. The dock lives in its own caller buffer, which must be 8-byte aligned:

```c
static uint64_t dock_memory[4096];
static const FuseClass panel = {.color = 0xFF1A1D22u, .pad_l = 8, .pad_t = 8};

if (fuse_dock_memory() > sizeof dock_memory) return 1;
FuseDock *dock = fuse_dock_create(dock_memory, sizeof dock_memory, 2);
if (!dock) return 1;
int scene = fuse_dock_register(dock, "scene", "Scene", 200, 120);
int props = fuse_dock_register(dock, "props", "Properties", 160, 120);
if (scene < 0 || props < 0 || !fuse_dock_place(dock, props, scene, FUSE_DOCK_RIGHT)) return 1;

/* Every frame, after fuse_canvas_clear(): */
FuseDockEvent event = {.x = mouse_x, .y = mouse_y, .press = pressed, .release = released};
fuse_dock_layout(dock, (FuseDockRect){0, 0, 1280, 720});
fuse_dock_event(dock, &event);
int window;
for (int i = 0; (window = fuse_dock_visible(dock, i)) >= 0; ++i) {
    fuse_dock_chrome(dock, ui, window, 0xFF1A1D22u, 0xFF2A2E35u, 0xFF3A404Au,
                     0xFFE0E0E0u, 0xFF808080u, 0xFF4A90E2u);
    if (fuse_dock_begin(dock, ui, window, &panel)) {
        /* build the panel's widgets here */
        fuse_dock_end(ui);
    }
}
fuse_dock_feedback(dock, ui, 0x804A90E2u);
```

`mouse_x`, `pressed` and the other event fields come from your platform layer. `fuse_dock_event()`
returns nonzero when the dock consumed the input, so you can keep it from the panels.
`fuse_dock_export()` and `fuse_dock_import()` save and restore the arrangement as a plain
`FuseDockLayout` value.

## Handling Errors

If a frame overflows a capacity, reuses an ID, or leaves a div or column open,
`fuse_canvas_draw()` returns NULL with a count of zero and cancels that frame's input.
`fuse_canvas_error()` reports the reason (`FUSE_ERR_OVERFLOW`, `FUSE_ERR_DUPLICATE_ID`,
`FUSE_ERR_UNBALANCED`), and the next `fuse_canvas_clear()` resets it. `fuse_canvas_debug(ui, true)`
overlays element boxes and a tree view of the frame.

See [Fuse symbols](/godstack/symbols/fuse/) for the generated declarations and header comments.


<!-- END PAGE: /godstack/docs/fuse/ -->

# Grit

Documentation: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/grit/
Markdown: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/grit.md
Description: Choose caller-backed allocators and use Grit utilities with explicit lifetimes.


# Grit

Grit is a collection of small utilities: arena, stack and pool allocators over memory you
provide, a dynamic array and a hash map, a seeded random number generator, fast approximate math
with vectors and 4x4 matrices, and a software rasterizer that draws into a pixel buffer. Each
part can be used on its own.

Define `GRIT_IMPLEMENTATION` in exactly one translation unit before including `Grit.h`. Other
translation units include the header without it. Define `GRIT_DEBUG` as well to turn on assertions
that catch misuse, such as freeing a pointer into the wrong allocator.

## Allocating from an Arena

The first thing to try is an arena: allocations come from one buffer, one after another, and are
all released together:

```c
#include <stdio.h>
#define GRIT_IMPLEMENTATION
#include "Grit.h"

int main(void)
{
    static unsigned char storage[1024];
    GritArena arena;
    grit_arena_init(&arena, storage, sizeof storage);

    int *squares = grit_arena_alloc(&arena, 10 * sizeof *squares);
    if (!squares) return 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; ++i) squares[i] = i * i;
    printf("squares[9] = %d, %zu bytes used\n", squares[9], arena.curr_offset);

    grit_arena_free_all(&arena);   /* every allocation is gone; storage is reusable */
    grit_arena_destroy(&arena);    /* detaches the arena; storage stays yours */
    return 0;
}
```

`grit_arena_init()` borrows your buffer; Grit never frees it. Each allocation is zeroed and
aligned to `GRIT_DEFAULT_ALIGN` (two pointers); `grit_arena_alloc_align()` takes an explicit
power-of-two alignment. When the buffer is full the call returns NULL rather than growing, so
check every result.

`grit_arena_resize()` grows or shrinks an allocation. The most recent allocation is resized in
place; any other is copied to a new block at the end of the arena. Arenas suit memory with one
shared lifetime, such as everything built during one frame or one request.

## Stack Allocation

A stack allocator also takes memory from a buffer, but can release the most recent allocations
first. `grit_stack_free()` rewinds the stack to just before the pointer you pass, releasing that
allocation and everything allocated after it:

```c
static unsigned char storage[4096];
GritStack stack;
grit_stack_init(&stack, storage, sizeof storage);

float *points = grit_stack_alloc(&stack, 256 * sizeof(float), 16);
char *scratch = grit_stack_alloc(&stack, 512, 1);
if (!points || !scratch) return 1;

grit_stack_free(&stack, scratch);   /* releases scratch */
grit_stack_free(&stack, points);    /* releases points */
```

The last argument of `grit_stack_alloc()` is the alignment (a power of two, at most 128). Each
allocation stores a small header in front of it so the stack knows how far to rewind.
`grit_stack_free_all()` empties it in one step.

## Pools of Equal-Sized Objects

A pool splits a buffer into equal chunks that can be allocated and freed in any order, which
suits objects that come and go, such as particles or connections:

```c
typedef struct Particle { float position[2], velocity[2]; uint32_t id; } Particle;

static unsigned char slots[4096];
GritPool pool;
grit_pool_init(&pool, slots, sizeof slots, sizeof(Particle), 16);

Particle *p = grit_pool_alloc(&pool);
if (!p) return 1;          /* every chunk is in use */
p->id = 7;
grit_pool_free(&pool, p);  /* the chunk can be handed out again */
```

The chunk size is rounded up to the alignment (here 20 bytes become 32, so the buffer holds up to 128
chunks) and must hold at least a pointer. Allocation and free are constant time; allocated chunks
are zeroed. With `GRIT_DEBUG` defined, allocating from an empty pool triggers an assertion instead
of returning NULL, which helps find undersized pools during development. `grit_pool_free_all()` returns every chunk.

## Dynamic Arrays and Hash Maps

`GritDArray` and `GritHashMap` grow as needed and, unlike the allocators, use `malloc()` and
`realloc()`. Both store fixed-size elements by copying their bytes:

```c
typedef struct Player { uint32_t id; int score; } Player;

GritDArray players = grit_darray_create(8, sizeof(Player));
GritHashMap by_id = grit_hashmap_create(16, sizeof(uint32_t), sizeof(size_t));

Player alice = {42, 1200};
grit_darray_push(&players, &alice);
size_t index = players.len - 1;
grit_hashmap_put(&by_id, &alice.id, &index);

uint32_t key = 42;
size_t *found = grit_hashmap_get(&by_id, &key);
if (found) {
    Player *player = grit_darray_get(&players, *found);
    player->score += 10;
}

grit_hashmap_del(&by_id, &key);
grit_hashmap_destroy(&by_id);
grit_darray_destroy(&players);
```

`grit_darray_get()` returns a pointer to the element, or NULL when the index is out of range; it
stays valid until the array grows. Pushes report nothing on allocation failure, so compare `len`
if it matters. `grit_darray_pop()` drops the last element.

Hash map keys are compared byte for byte. Integers work directly; for structs, zero the whole key
(including padding) before filling it, and store strings in fixed-size buffers. `put` copies the
value and replaces an existing one; `get` returns a pointer to the stored value, or NULL. Pointers
returned by `get` are invalidated when the map grows.

## Random Numbers

`GritRng` is a small, fast xorshift generator. The same seed always gives the same sequence,
which makes simulations reproducible. It is not suitable for cryptography:

```c
GritRng rng;
grit_rng_seed(&rng, 1234);
uint32_t roll = grit_rng_u32(&rng) % 6 + 1;
float t;
grit_rng_f32(&rng, &t);   /* uniform in [0, 1) */
```

## Vectors and Matrices

The math functions favor speed over accuracy and write through their first argument instead of
returning values. Vectors are `float[2]` and `float[3]`; matrices are `float[16]` in column-major
order:

```c
float eye[3], center[3], up[3], offset[3];
grit_vec3f(eye, 0, 2, 5);
grit_vec3f(center, 0, 0, 0);
grit_vec3f(up, 0, 1, 0);
grit_vec3f(offset, 1, 0, 0);

float model[16], view[16], mvp[16];
grit_mat4_translate(model, offset);
grit_mat4_rotate_y_by(model, GRIT_PI * 0.25f);
grit_mat4_lookat(view, eye, center, up);
grit_mat4_perspective(mvp, GRIT_PI / 3, 16.0f / 9.0f, 0.1f, 100.0f);
grit_mat4_mul(mvp, view);    /* mvp = projection * view */
grit_mat4_mul(mvp, model);   /* mvp = projection * view * model */
```

`grit_mat4_mul(a, b)` stores `a * b` in `a`, and the `_by` variants multiply an existing matrix
by a translation or rotation. The perspective matrix is right-handed and maps depth to `0..1`, as
Vulkan expects. `grit_sinf()`, `grit_cosf()`, `grit_atan2f()` and the vector lengths are
approximations: good for animation and graphics, not for numerics.

## Drawing Pixels

`GritDraw` draws into a buffer of `0xAARRGGBB` pixels that you own, row by row with no padding.
Colors are written as given, without blending. This program draws a small scene and saves it as a
PPM image:

```c
#include <stdio.h>
#define GRIT_IMPLEMENTATION
#include "Grit.h"

enum { W = 160, H = 100 };

int main(void)
{
    static uint32_t pixels[W * H];
    GritDraw d;
    grit_draw_begin(&d, pixels, W, H);

    grit_draw_clear(&d, 0xFF101418u);
    grit_draw_rect_gradient(&d, 0, 0, W, 40, 0xFF203050u, 0xFF203050u, 0xFF101418u, 0xFF101418u);
    grit_draw_tri(&d, 20, 90, 60, 30, 100, 90, 0xFFFF0000u, 0xFF00FF00u, 0xFF0000FFu);
    grit_draw_line(&d, 0, 95, W - 1, 60, 2, 0xFFFFFFFFu, 0xFFFFAA00u);
    grit_draw_clip(&d, 110, 20, 40, 40);
    grit_draw_circle(&d, 130, 40, 30, 0xFFFFD040u);   /* clipped to the 40x40 box */
    grit_draw_clip_reset(&d);

    FILE *out = fopen("grit.ppm", "wb");
    if (!out) return 1;
    fprintf(out, "P6\n%d %d\n255\n", W, H);
    for (int i = 0; i < W * H; ++i) {
        unsigned char rgb[3] = {(pixels[i] >> 16) & 0xFF, (pixels[i] >> 8) & 0xFF, pixels[i] & 0xFF};
        fwrite(rgb, 1, 3, out);
    }
    return fclose(out) == 0 ? 0 : 1;
}
```

Every primitive clips to the buffer and to the rectangle set with `grit_draw_clip()`, except
`grit_draw_clear()`, which fills the whole buffer. Gradient corners run top-left, top-right,
bottom-right, bottom-left; triangles interpolate their three vertex colors; lines take a width and
blend from the first color to the second. `grit_draw_blit()` copies a block of pixels and
`grit_draw_pixel()` sets one. To show the result in a window, upload the buffer with your platform
layer, as the [Grit demo](https://github.com/godxgun/godstack/tree/main/demos/grit) does with
[Peak](/godstack/docs/peak/).

See [Grit symbols](/godstack/symbols/grit/) for the generated declarations.


<!-- END PAGE: /godstack/docs/grit/ -->

<!-- BEGIN PAGE: /godstack/docs/peak/ -->
# Peak

Documentation: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/peak/
Markdown: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/peak.md
Description: Set up Peak runtime contexts and a platform event loop with target-specific dependencies.


# Peak

Peak is a platform layer that abstracts operating-system windowing and related services behind
a C API. Platform-specific implementations are selected at compile time; some system libraries
are loaded at runtime.

## Opening a Window

The first thing to try is opening a window and setting up an event loop. You can poll events with
`peak_window_epoll`, or let `peak_window_run` call a tick callback.

### A Basic Event Loop
```c
#define PEAK_IMPLEMENTATION
#include "Peak.h"
int main(void) {
    PeakCtx *ctx = peak_init();
    if (!ctx) return 1;

    PeakWindow window = peak_window_open(ctx, "My Window", 888, 333, 0);
    if (!window.ctx) {
        peak_quit(ctx);
        return 1;
    }

    PeakEvent event;
    bool running = true;
    while (running) {
        while (peak_window_epoll(&window, &event)) {
            if (event.type == PEAK_EVENT_WINDOW_CLOSE) running = false;
        }
    }

    peak_window_close(&window);
    peak_quit(ctx);
    return 0;
}
```

The context owns Peak's runtime state and is required when opening a window. Call `peak_init()`
to create it and `peak_quit(ctx)` when done. Peak manages its runtime storage internally.

### With The Callback API

The callback API helps portability on platforms such as the web, where the browser owns the
main loop. `peak_window_run()` repeatedly calls your callback on native platforms and registers
it with the browser main loop on Web.


```c
static int tick(PeakWindow *window, void *userdata) {
    PeakEvent event;
    (void)userdata;
    while (peak_window_epoll(window, &event)) {
        if (event.type == PEAK_EVENT_WINDOW_CLOSE) return 0;
    }
    return 1;
}

int main(void) {
    PeakCtx *ctx = peak_init();
    if (!ctx) return 1;
    PeakWindow window = peak_window_open(ctx, "My Window", 888, 333, 0);
    if (window.ctx) {
        peak_window_run(&window, tick, NULL);
        peak_window_close(&window);
    }
    peak_quit(ctx);
    return 0;
}
```

## Using the Filesystem

The basic file helpers use paths from the process working directory. `peak_file_alloc()` returns
a heap buffer; release it with `free()`. The filesystem helpers return nonzero on success.

```c
const char message[] = "hello from Peak\n";
const char *path = "peak-note.txt";

if (!peak_file_write(path, message, sizeof(message) - 1)) return 1;

unsigned long size = 0;
char *contents = peak_file_alloc(path, &size);
if (!contents) return 1;
fwrite(contents, 1, size, stdout);
free(contents);

if (!peak_filesystem_rename(path, "peak-note-copy.txt")) return 1;
if (!peak_filesystem_rm("peak-note-copy.txt")) return 1;
```

Use `peak_filesystem_cwd()` and `peak_filesystem_chdir()` to inspect or change the working
directory. `peak_filesystem_mkdir()` creates one directory level, and `peak_filesystem_list()`
calls your callback for each entry. For bounded, directory-handle-based I/O on supported Linux
systems, see the `peak_io_*` API in the [symbol reference](/godstack/symbols/peak/).

## Spawning a TTY

`peak_pty_spawn()` starts a child attached to a pseudoterminal and returns its nonblocking file
handle and process ID. Pass the executable and a NULL-terminated argument vector. This example
uses the POSIX shell; choose a host-appropriate executable and arguments for other systems.

```c
const char *argv[] = {"/bin/sh", NULL};
PeakProc tty = peak_pty_spawn("/bin/sh", argv, 80, 24, 0, 0);
if (tty.fd == PEAK_HANDLE_INVALID) return 1;

const char command[] = "printf 'hello from the child\\n'; exit\n";
if (peak_fd_write(tty.fd, command, sizeof(command) - 1) < 0) {
    peak_pty_close(&tty);
    return 1;
}

char output[256];
for (;;) {
    int n = peak_fd_read(tty.fd, output, sizeof(output));
    if (n > 0) fwrite(output, 1, (size_t)n, stdout);
    else if (n == 0) break; /* child closed the terminal */
    else if (peak_pty_reap(&tty)) break; /* no data and child has exited */
    else peak_sleep_ns(1000000); /* -1: no data available yet */
}
while (!peak_pty_reap(&tty)) peak_sleep_ns(1000000);
peak_pty_close(&tty);
```

Use `peak_pty_resize()` when the terminal dimensions change. `peak_pty_reap()` reports when the
child exits; `peak_pty_close()` releases the PTY and any remaining process resources.

## Memory Mapped Circular Ring Buffer

`peak_mirror_map()` maps the same storage twice in adjacent address ranges. The requested size
must be a multiple of `peak_page_size()`. The returned pointer can be indexed across the wrap
boundary without splitting a copy; the valid mapped range is `size * 2` bytes.

```c
size_t size = peak_page_size();
unsigned char *ring = peak_mirror_map(size);
if (!ring) return 1;

/* This contiguous write crosses the ring boundary at `size`. */
memcpy(ring + size - 3, "abcdef", 6);
/* The bytes are also visible at ring[0..2] through the second mapping. */

peak_mirror_unmap(ring, size);
```

Keep the original `size` for `peak_mirror_unmap()` and do not access the mapping after unmapping.

## Streaming Audio

`peak_audio_start()` asks the audio device to pull interleaved signed 16-bit samples. The callback
receives a frame count, so write `frames * channels` samples. Keep it real-time safe: avoid
blocking, file I/O, and allocation in the callback. It returns nonzero when the stream starts;
call `peak_audio_stop()` to stop it. With `PEAK_NO_AUDIO`, starting audio returns zero.

```c
static void fill_audio(int16_t *out, size_t frames, void *userdata) {
    uint32_t *phase = userdata;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < frames; ++i) {
        *phase = (*phase + 440) % 48000;
        out[i] = (*phase % 48000) < 24000 ? 8000 : -8000;
    }
}

uint32_t phase = 0;
if (!peak_audio_start(1, 48000, fill_audio, &phase)) return 1;
/* ... play ... */
peak_audio_stop();
```



<!-- END PAGE: /godstack/docs/peak/ -->

<!-- BEGIN PAGE: /godstack/docs/poof/ -->
# Poof

Documentation: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/poof/
Markdown: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/poof.md
Description: Construct process commands and compiler configurations with Poof.


# Poof

Poof lets you write a project's build script in C. You keep a `build.c` next to your sources,
compile it once with `cc build.c -o build`, and from then on run `./build`. Poof provides
commands, a compiler description that becomes GCC, Clang, MinGW or MSVC command lines, parallel
batches, file helpers and a self-rebuild macro.

Every function is `static`, so no implementation macro is needed. Include `Poof.h` before any C
library header: it defines `_POSIX_C_SOURCE` (and `_DARWIN_C_SOURCE` on macOS) for the process
APIs it uses.

## Running a Command

The first thing to try is running one program and checking that it succeeded:

```c
#include "Poof.h"

int main(void)
{
    Poof_Cmd cmd = {0};
    poof_cmd_append(&cmd, "cc", "--version");
    bool ok = poof_cmd_run(&cmd);
    poof_cmd_free(&cmd);
    return ok ? 0 : 1;
}
```

`Poof_Cmd` is a growable list of argument pointers. `poof_cmd_append()` takes any number of
strings; it stores the pointers, not copies, so each string must stay alive while the command is
used. `poof_cmd_run()` joins the arguments into one command line, quoting arguments that contain
spaces, prints it, and runs it with the system shell. It returns `true` when the exit status is
zero and then empties the command, keeping its storage for reuse. `poof_cmd_free()` releases the
storage.

Because the command line goes through the shell, do not build commands from untrusted input.

## Compiling a Program

A `Poof_CC` describes one compilation: inputs, output, include paths, defines, libraries and
flags. `poof_cc_run()` turns it into a compiler command line, runs it, and frees the
configuration:

```c
Poof_CC cc;
poof_cc_init(&cc, poof_has_cmd("clang") ? POOF_CC_CLANG : POOF_CC_GCC, POOF_TARGET_HOST);
cc.output = "app";
cc.optimization = POOF_O2;
cc.debug_mode = false;
poof_cmd_append(&cc.inputs, "app.c");
poof_cmd_append(&cc.includes, ".");
poof_cmd_append(&cc.defines, "NDEBUG");
poof_cmd_append(&cc.libs, "m");
poof_cmd_append(&cc.extra_flags, "-std=c99", "-Wall", "-Wextra");
if (!poof_cc_run(&cc)) return 1;
```

With Clang this runs roughly
`clang -target ... -O2 -DNDEBUG -I. app.c -o app -lm -std=c99 -Wall -Wextra`. Includes, defines
and libraries are written without their `-I`, `-D` and `-l` prefixes; Poof adds the right
spelling for the compiler, including `/I`, `/D` and `name.lib` for MSVC. Flags in `extra_flags`
are passed through unchanged.

`poof_cc_init()` starts in debug mode (`-g`) at `POOF_O0`. `optimization` combines one level
(`POOF_O0` to `POOF_O3`) with optional instruction-set flags such as `POOF_AVX2` or `POOF_BMI`.
The compiler argument is a bit mask; when several bits are set, Poof uses the first of GCC,
Clang, MinGW and MSVC. `poof_cc_available()` probes which compilers are installed and returns
that mask, and `poof_has_cmd()` checks for any program on the `PATH`.

## Platform Flags and Cross Targets

Flags that only apply to one operating system go into `win32_flags`, `linux_flags` or
`macos_flags`, usually through the matching macros. Only the collection for the target being
built is used:

```c
Poof_CC cc;
poof_cc_init(&cc, POOF_CC_CLANG, POOF_TARGET_LINUX | POOF_TARGET_WIN32);
cc.output = "tool";
poof_cmd_append(&cc.inputs, "tool.c");
poof_cc_append_linux(&cc, "-ldl", "-lpthread");
poof_cc_append_win32(&cc, "-lgdi32");
if (!poof_cc_run(&cc)) return 1;
```

`POOF_TARGET_HOST` builds for the running system. A mask with several targets produces one
compiler command per target and suffixes the output names (`tool_linux`, `tool_win32.exe`).
Clang selects targets with `-target`; GCC switches to `x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc` for Windows. macOS
builds compile sources as Objective-C so that AppKit headers work.

## Building in Parallel

A `Poof_Batch` collects commands and runs them concurrently. `poof_batch_append_cc()` converts a
compiler description into commands and frees the description; `poof_batch_append()` adds a
`Poof_Cmd`, and the batch takes ownership of it:

```c
Poof_Batch batch = {0};

Poof_Cmd shader = {0};
poof_cmd_append(&shader, "slangc", "ui.slang", "-target", "spirv", "-o", "ui.spv");
poof_batch_append(&batch, shader);

const char *programs[] = {"server", "client"};
const char *sources[] = {"server.c", "client.c"};
for (int i = 0; i < 2; ++i) {
    Poof_CC cc;
    poof_cc_init(&cc, POOF_CC_GCC, POOF_TARGET_HOST);
    cc.output = programs[i];
    poof_cmd_append(&cc.inputs, sources[i]);
    poof_batch_append_cc(&batch, &cc);
}

if (!poof_batch_run(&batch, "build")) return 1;
```

`poof_batch_run()` starts one job per CPU, draws a progress bar labelled `build`, waits for every
command, and frees the batch. It returns `false` if any command failed.
`poof_batch_run_parallel()` takes an explicit job limit. Commands in one batch must not depend on
each other; run dependent steps in separate batches.

## Skipping Up-to-Date Work

`poof_needs_rebuild()` compares modification times and returns `true` when the target is missing
or older than any source. The file helpers return `true` on success:

```c
const char *inputs[] = {"app.c", "app.h"};
if (!poof_mkdir("bin")) return 1;
if (poof_needs_rebuild("bin/app", inputs, 2)) {
    Poof_CC cc;
    poof_cc_init(&cc, POOF_CC_GCC, POOF_TARGET_HOST);
    cc.output = "bin/app";
    poof_cmd_append(&cc.inputs, "app.c");
    if (!poof_cc_run(&cc)) return 1;
}
if (!poof_copy_file("README.md", "bin/README.md")) return 1;
```

`poof_touch()`, `poof_rm()` and `poof_rm_recursive()` cover the remaining file housekeeping.

## Rebuilding the Build Script

Put `POOF_GO_REBUILD_URSELF(argc, argv)` at the start of `main()`. When the build script's source
file is newer than the running executable, Poof renames the old binary to `<name>.old`,
recompiles the script with `gcc`, and executes the new binary with the same arguments:

```c
#include "Poof.h"

int main(int argc, char **argv)
{
    POOF_GO_REBUILD_URSELF(argc, argv);

    Poof_CC cc;
    poof_cc_init(&cc, POOF_CC_GCC, POOF_TARGET_HOST);
    cc.output = "app";
    poof_cmd_append(&cc.inputs, "app.c");
    return poof_cc_run(&cc) ? 0 : 1;
}
```

After the first `cc build.c -o build`, editing `build.c` and running `./build` is enough.

## Printing Status

`poof_print()` is `printf` with a 24-bit `0xRRGGBB` color that is applied only when standard
output is a terminal. `poof_support()` prints a list of name and yes/no pairs, then the host's
SIMD support, and returns the SIMD flags as `POOF_*` optimization bits:

```c
poof_print(0x00FF88, "[build] %d targets\n", 2);
uint32_t simd = poof_support("app", "Vulkan", poof_has_cmd("glslangValidator"));
if (POOF_IS_SET(simd, POOF_AVX2)) poof_print(0x888888, "using AVX2 paths\n");
```

This repository's own [`build.c`](https://github.com/godxgun/godstack/blob/main/build.c) is a
full example: run `cc build.c -o build` and then `./build demo <name>` from the repository root.

See [Poof symbols](/godstack/symbols/poof/) for all declarations.


<!-- END PAGE: /godstack/docs/poof/ -->

# Rend

Documentation: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/rend/
Markdown: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/rend.md
Description: Use legacy Rend with Peak on native Vulkan and browser WebGL2.


# Rend

Rend provides one graphics API for its supported backends. `REND_BACKEND_AUTO` selects WebGL2
when compiled with Emscripten and Vulkan 1.4 on native builds that enable `PEAK_VULKAN`.

The supported graphics backends are Vulkan 1.4 and Emscripten WebGL2. DirectX 12 and Metal
selections are currently unavailable. Rend uses Peak for window creation and platform setup.

Put the implementation macros in exactly one C translation unit. Other translation units include
the headers without those macros. `PEAK_VULKAN` enables the native Vulkan backend and should be
omitted for Emscripten:

```c
#if !defined(__EMSCRIPTEN__)
#define PEAK_VULKAN
#endif
#define PEAK_IMPLEMENTATION
#include "Peak.h"
#define REND_IMPLEMENTATION
#include "Rend.h"
```

See the [Peak guide](/godstack/docs/peak/) for platform dependencies and window setup.

## Creating a Renderer

Create Peak first, then open a window and attach a Rend renderer to it. Pass `REND_BACKEND_AUTO`
to use the platform default. The renderer owns its frame and presentation state; destroy it
before closing its Peak window, then release Peak.

```c
PeakCtx *peak = peak_init();
if (!peak) return 1;

PeakWindow window = peak_window_open(peak, "Rend", 960, 540, 0);
if (!window.ctx) {
    peak_quit(peak);
    return 1;
}

RendBindingInfo bindings = {0};
RendRenderer renderer = rend_renderer_create(
    &window, REND_BACKEND_AUTO, NULL, true, &bindings);
if (!renderer) {
    peak_window_close(&window);
    peak_quit(peak);
    return 1;
}

/* Render frames here. */

rend_renderer_destroy(renderer);
rend_quit();
peak_window_close(&window);
peak_quit(peak);
```

`rend_renderer_frame_begin()` acquires a frame and can fail, for example when the window is
being resized. Record render commands only after it succeeds, then call
`rend_renderer_frame_end()` to submit and present. For headless work, use
`rend_renderer_create_offscreen()` instead of opening a window.

## Creating your first Pipeline

Graphics pipelines combine shader stages with vertex input and fixed state. Vulkan pipelines use
SPIR-V; WebGL2 pipelines use GLSL ES 3.00. `rend_pipeline_create_graphics_portable()` accepts both
shader forms and selects the one for the active backend. Supply equivalent shaders for both
backends: the GLSL below is the WebGL2 version, while Vulkan needs separately compiled SPIR-V.
The vertex binding gives the byte stride; attributes map shader locations to fields in each vertex.

This example uses a 2D position and a 16-byte push-constant color. The Vulkan SPIR-V shaders must
use the same vertex location and push-constant layout as the WebGL2 shaders:

```glsl
// Vertex shader
#version 300 es
layout(location=0) in vec2 position;
void main() { gl_Position = vec4(position, 0.0, 1.0); }
```

```glsl
// Fragment shader
#version 300 es
precision mediump float;
layout(std140) uniform RendPushConstants { vec4 color; };
out vec4 fragColor;
void main() { fragColor = color; }
```

Create the pipeline after creating the renderer. `REND_FORMAT_UNDEFINED` uses the renderer's
default color target format; depth testing is disabled here.

```c
static const RendVertexBinding vertex_binding = {
    0, sizeof(float) * 2, REND_INPUT_RATE_VERTEX
};
static const RendVertexAttributes position_attribute = {
    0, 0, 0, REND_FORMAT_2_SFLOAT32
};
static const RendPushConstantInfo color_constant = {0, sizeof(float) * 4};

RendPipeline pipeline = rend_pipeline_create_graphics_portable(
    renderer,
    vertex_spirv, vertex_spirv_size,
    fragment_spirv, fragment_spirv_size,
    vertex_glsl, fragment_glsl,
    &vertex_binding, 1,
    &position_attribute, 1,
    &color_constant, 1,
    REND_POLYGON_MODE_FILL, REND_CULL_MODE_NONE,
    REND_TOPOLOGY_TRIANGLE_LIST, REND_FORMAT_UNDEFINED, false);
if (!pipeline) return 1;
```

Store the GLSL examples in C strings named `vertex_glsl` and `fragment_glsl`. Load or embed the
separately compiled Vulkan artifacts as `vertex_spirv` and `fragment_spirv`; pass each artifact's
size in bytes. The push-constant range must match the data sent when drawing.

## Drawing a triangle

Create a vertex buffer, write three positions, and bind it while recording a frame. The push
constant color is passed to the shader before drawing.

```c
static const float triangle[] = {
     0.0f, -0.6f,
    -0.6f,  0.5f,
     0.6f,  0.5f,
};
float color[4] = {0.2f, 0.7f, 1.0f, 1.0f};

RendBuffer vertices = rend_buffer_create(
    renderer, sizeof triangle, REND_BUFFER_VERTEX, true);
if (!vertices.handle) return 1;
rend_buffer_write(renderer, &vertices, triangle, sizeof triangle, 0);

if (rend_renderer_frame_begin(renderer)) {
    rend_cmd_render_begin(renderer, 0.05f, 0.06f, 0.08f, 1.0f);
    rend_cmd_bind_pipeline(pipeline);
    rend_cmd_bind_vertex_buffer(pipeline, 0, vertices, 0);
    rend_cmd_push_constants(pipeline, color, sizeof color);
    rend_cmd_draw(pipeline, 3, 1);
    rend_cmd_render_end(renderer);
    rend_renderer_frame_end(renderer, NULL);
}

```

The draw count is the number of vertices; the final argument is the instance count. Keep buffers
alive while submitted GPU work may still reference them. Release them when they are no longer in
use, or let `rend_quit()` release all Rend objects, including buffers and pipelines.

## Drawing a Mesh

For indexed meshes, store vertex attributes in one or more vertex buffers and triangle indices
in an index buffer. Bind both buffers and issue `rend_cmd_draw_indexed()`. The vertex layout in
the pipeline must match the fields in your vertex structure.

```c
typedef struct MeshVertex { float position[2]; } MeshVertex;

static const MeshVertex mesh_vertices[] = {
    {{-0.6f, -0.5f}}, {{-0.6f, 0.5f}},
    {{ 0.6f, -0.5f}}, {{ 0.6f, 0.5f}},
};
static const uint16_t mesh_indices[] = {0, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3};

RendBuffer vertex_buffer = rend_buffer_create(
    renderer, sizeof mesh_vertices, REND_BUFFER_VERTEX, true);
RendBuffer index_buffer = rend_buffer_create(
    renderer, sizeof mesh_indices, REND_BUFFER_INDEX, true);
if (!vertex_buffer.handle || !index_buffer.handle) return 1;
rend_buffer_write(renderer, &vertex_buffer, mesh_vertices, sizeof mesh_vertices, 0);
rend_buffer_write(renderer, &index_buffer, mesh_indices, sizeof mesh_indices, 0);

if (rend_renderer_frame_begin(renderer)) {
    rend_cmd_render_begin(renderer, 0.05f, 0.06f, 0.08f, 1.0f);
    rend_cmd_bind_pipeline(pipeline);
    rend_cmd_bind_vertex_buffer(pipeline, 0, vertex_buffer, 0);
    rend_cmd_bind_index_buffer(pipeline, index_buffer, 0, REND_INDEX_UINT16);
    rend_cmd_draw_indexed(pipeline, 6, 0, 0, 1);
    rend_cmd_render_end(renderer);
    rend_renderer_frame_end(renderer, NULL);
}

```

This mesh reuses the position-only pipeline from the triangle example. For a richer vertex
structure, update the binding stride and add attributes with their matching shader locations and
`offsetof()` values. `first_index` selects the starting index, `vertex_offset` is added to each
index, and the final argument is the instance count. Keep both buffers alive while submitted GPU
work may reference them. The same buffers and draw commands work with Vulkan and WebGL2 when the
pipeline provides the matching shader for each backend.



<!-- END PAGE: /godstack/docs/rend/ -->

<!-- BEGIN PAGE: /godstack/docs/type/ -->
# Type

Documentation: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/type/
Markdown: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/type.md
Description: Place a Type context, load font bytes, and lay out and rasterize glyphs into a coverage atlas.


# Type

Type turns font files and UTF-8 text into positioned glyphs. It parses TrueType and OpenType
fonts (`glyf`, CFF and CFF2 outlines, and font collections), rasterizes glyphs with its own
antialiased rasterizer, and packs them into a coverage atlas that your renderer uploads as a
texture. Each glyph you get back says where it is in the atlas and where to draw it.

Type does not read files and does not allocate. Its state lives in a buffer you provide, font
bytes are borrowed from you, and temporary work uses a scratch buffer you attach. Font data is
validated with bounded reads, so a malformed or hostile font is rejected with an error instead of
being trusted.

Define `TYPE_IMPLEMENTATION` in exactly one translation unit before including `Type.h`, and link
with `-lm`.

## Creating a Context

The first thing to try is placing a context. The parameters fix the atlas size, the glyph cache
and how many faces the context can hold:

```c
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#define TYPE_IMPLEMENTATION
#include "Type.h"

int main(void)
{
    TypeParams params;
    type_params_default(&params);
    size_t bytes = type_memory(&params);
    if (!bytes || bytes > SIZE_MAX - 15) return 1;

    void *memory = malloc(bytes + 15);
    if (!memory) return 1;
    void *aligned = (void *)(((uintptr_t)memory + 15) & ~(uintptr_t)15);

    TypeCtx *ctx = type_place(aligned, bytes, &params);
    if (!ctx) {
        free(memory);
        return 1;
    }
    printf("%ux%u atlas, %u cached glyphs, up to %u faces: %zu bytes\n",
           params.atlas_width, params.atlas_height, params.cache_capacity,
           params.max_faces, bytes);
    free(memory);
    return 0;
}
```

`type_params_default()` fills in a 1024x1024 atlas, a 2048-glyph cache, eight faces and eight
fallbacks with box-filter antialiasing. `type_memory()` returns the bytes those parameters need,
or zero if they are unusable, and `type_place()` builds the context in your buffer. The buffer
must be 16-byte aligned, which is why the example rounds the pointer up. Nothing in the context
grows later; to change a limit, place a new context. There is no destroy call: free the buffer
when you are done.

## Rendering Text

With a context in place, add a font, attach scratch memory, and lay out a line. This program
loads the font named on the command line and prints a string as ASCII art:

```c
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#define TYPE_IMPLEMENTATION
#include "Type.h"

enum { COLS = 100, ROWS = 24 };

static unsigned char font_bytes[16 << 20];
static unsigned char scratch_bytes[1 << 20];
static char picture[ROWS][COLS + 1];

int main(int argc, char **argv)
{
    if (argc < 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "usage: %s font.ttf\n", argv[0]);
        return 2;
    }
    FILE *file = fopen(argv[1], "rb");
    if (!file) return 1;
    size_t font_len = fread(font_bytes, 1, sizeof font_bytes, file);
    fclose(file);

    TypeParams params;
    type_params_default(&params);
    size_t bytes = type_memory(&params);
    void *memory = bytes ? malloc(bytes + 15) : NULL;
    if (!memory) return 1;
    TypeCtx *ctx = type_place((void *)(((uintptr_t)memory + 15) & ~(uintptr_t)15), bytes, &params);

    uint32_t font_id;
    TypeError error = ctx ? type_add_font(ctx, font_bytes, font_len, NULL, &font_id)
                          : TYPE_ERR_BUF_TOO_SMALL;
    if (error != TYPE_OK) {
        fprintf(stderr, "cannot use %s: error %d\n", argv[1], (int)error);
        free(memory);
        return 1;
    }

    TypeScratch scratch;
    type_scratch_init(&scratch, scratch_bytes, sizeof scratch_bytes);
    type_set_scratch(ctx, &scratch);

    const char text[] = "Hello, Type!";
    const float size = 20.0f;
    TypeCell cells[64];
    uint32_t count = 0;
    TypeMetrics metrics;
    error = type_layout_utf8(ctx, text, sizeof text - 1, size, cells, 64, &count, NULL);
    if (error == TYPE_OK) error = type_metrics(ctx, size, &metrics);
    type_set_scratch(ctx, NULL);
    if (error != TYPE_OK) {
        free(memory);
        return 1;
    }

    uint32_t atlas_w, atlas_h;
    const uint8_t *atlas = type_ctx_atlas(ctx, &atlas_w, &atlas_h);
    int baseline = (int)(metrics.ascender + 0.5f);
    memset(picture, ' ', sizeof picture);
    for (uint32_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
        const TypeGlyph *g = &cells[i].glyph;
        int left = (int)(cells[i].x + g->bearing_x);
        int top = baseline + (int)cells[i].y - (int)g->bearing_y;
        for (int y = 0; y < g->height; ++y)
            for (int x = 0; x < g->width; ++x) {
                uint8_t coverage = atlas[(size_t)(g->atlas_y + y) * atlas_w + g->atlas_x + x];
                int px = left + x, py = top + y;
                if (coverage > 64 && px >= 0 && px < COLS && py >= 0 && py < ROWS)
                    picture[py][px] = coverage > 160 ? '#' : '+';
            }
    }
    for (int row = 0; row < ROWS; ++row) {
        picture[row][COLS] = '\0';
        puts(picture[row]);
    }
    free(memory);
    return 0;
}
```

Build it with `cc -std=c99 -Wall -Wextra -I. hello_type.c -lm -o hello_type` and run
`./hello_type path/to/font.ttf`.

`type_add_font()` validates the font and returns an ID. Type keeps pointers into `font_bytes`, so
those bytes must stay alive and unchanged until `type_clear_fonts()` or until the context is
discarded. The first font added becomes the primary face. For a collection (`.ttc`), the first
face is used.

`type_layout_utf8()` lays out one line starting at the origin, with the baseline at `y = 0`. Each
`TypeCell` holds the codepoint, the pen position `x`, `y`, and a `TypeGlyph`. A glyph's image is
the rectangle `atlas_x`, `atlas_y`, `width`, `height` in the coverage atlas, and is drawn with its
left edge at `x + bearing_x` and its top edge at `y - bearing_y` (bearings point up from the
baseline). `type_metrics()` gives the primary face's ascender, descender and line gap at a pixel
size, for placing the baseline and spacing lines; the descender is negative, so the distance
between baselines is `ascender - descender + line_gap`. Sizes are rounded to whole pixels.

## Scratch Memory

Rasterizing a glyph that is not yet in the atlas needs temporary memory. `type_scratch_init()`
wraps a buffer you own, and `type_set_scratch()` lends it to the context until you pass NULL.
Without scratch, uncached glyphs fail with `TYPE_ERR_SCRATCH_REQUIRED`; if the buffer is too
small they fail with `TYPE_ERR_SCRATCH_FULL`.

Every call releases what it took from scratch before returning, so the buffer can be a per-frame
arena. Detach it before you reset or reuse that memory. `scratch.peak` records the most a call has
needed, which is a good guide for sizing. Cached glyphs need no scratch at all.

## Uploading the Atlas

Glyphs are packed into the atlas as they are first requested. The atlas is one byte of coverage
per pixel, `atlas_w * atlas_h` bytes, row by row:

```c
static uint64_t uploaded_revision;

uint32_t w, h;
const uint8_t *pixels = type_ctx_atlas(ctx, &w, &h);
uint64_t revision = type_ctx_atlas_revision(ctx);
if (revision != uploaded_revision) {
    upload_texture_r8(texture, pixels, w, h);   /* your renderer */
    uploaded_revision = revision;
}
```

The revision changes only when atlas pixels change, so cache hits cost no upload. Each texture
that mirrors the atlas tracks its own revision.

Printable ASCII and U+FFFD are kept in a fast table for the current size; the first request at a
new size rasterizes that whole set. Other glyphs live in an LRU cache of `cache_capacity`
entries. When the atlas has no room left, requests fail with `TYPE_ERR_ATLAS_FULL`;
`type_clear_atlas()` empties the atlas and cache so you can start over.

## Faces, Styles and Fallbacks

A context can hold several faces. Pass `TypeFaceParams` to mark a face as the bold, italic or
bold-italic member of the family, and list faces to try when the primary face has no glyph for a
codepoint:

```c
uint32_t regular, bold, symbols;
TypeFaceParams bold_face;
type_face_params_default(&bold_face);
bold_face.style.bold = 1;
bold_face.weight = TYPE_WEIGHT_BOLD;

if (type_add_font(ctx, regular_bytes, regular_len, NULL, &regular) != TYPE_OK) return 1;
if (type_add_font(ctx, bold_bytes, bold_len, &bold_face, &bold) != TYPE_OK) return 1;
if (type_add_font(ctx, symbol_bytes, symbol_len, NULL, &symbols) != TYPE_OK) return 1;
if (type_set_fallbacks(ctx, &symbols, 1) != TYPE_OK) return 1;

TypeStyle strong = {.italic = 0, .bold = 1};
TypeGlyph glyph;
TypeError error = type_glyph_styled(ctx, 'A', 18.0f, strong, &glyph);
```

`type_glyph()` and `type_glyph_styled()` return one glyph, rasterizing it if needed. A styled
request uses the matching style face, then the primary face, then the fallbacks in order. A
codepoint no face has is drawn with the primary face's `.notdef` glyph (glyph ID 0).
`type_select()` changes the primary face, and `type_peek_glyph()` checks the cache without
rasterizing.

## Shaped Text

`type_layout_utf8()` maps each codepoint to one glyph. It does not form ligatures, reorder
right-to-left text, place combining marks or wrap lines. For complex scripts, run a shaper such as
HarfBuzz first and pass its output to Type as `TypeShapedGlyph` records:

```c
TypeShapedGlyph run[] = {
    /* font_id, glyph_id, cluster, x_advance, y_advance, x_offset, y_offset */
    {regular, 73, 0, 11.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f},
    {regular, 89, 2, 9.5f, 0.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f},
};
TypePositionedGlyph placed[2];
uint32_t written = 0;
TypeTextMetrics ink;

if (type_layout_shaped(ctx, run, 2, 20.0f, placed, 2, &written, &ink) != TYPE_OK) return 1;
/* placed[i].x and placed[i].y are pen positions; ink.advance_x is the run width */
```

Glyph IDs, clusters (byte offsets into your text) and fractional advances come straight from the
shaper, in visual order and with y pointing down. `type_measure_shaped()` computes the same
advance and ink bounds without rasterizing anything, which suits line breaking. The
[`demos/type/`](https://github.com/godxgun/godstack/tree/main/demos/type) fixtures include a
HarfBuzz and FriBidi bridge.

## Lower-Level Building Blocks

The context is built from parts you can also use directly. `type_ttf_place()` parses font bytes
into a buffer of `type_ttf_memory()` bytes, and `type_font_from_ttf()` makes a face from it. A
face answers metric and glyph questions and renders single glyphs into your own memory:

```c
uint16_t glyph_id;
TypeBitmap info;
if (type_font_glyph_index(font, 'g', &glyph_id) != TYPE_OK) return 1;
if (type_font_bitmap_info(font, glyph_id, 32.0f, &info) != TYPE_OK) return 1;

size_t size = type_bitmap_bytes(&info);
uint8_t *coverage = malloc(size ? size : 1);
if (!coverage) return 1;
TypeError error = type_font_render_bitmap_scratch(font, glyph_id, 32.0f, TYPE_AA_BOX,
                                                  coverage, size, &scratch, &info);
```

`type_font_outline()` returns the glyph outline as move, line, quadratic and cubic segments in
font units, for tessellation or vector export. The atlas packer is available on its own as well:
`type_atlas_place()`, `type_atlas_pack()` and `type_atlas_blit()` shelf-pack any coverage images
into a buffer you provide.

`type_utf8_next()` decodes one codepoint and returns its byte length, or zero for an invalid or
truncated sequence; `type_utf8_validate()` checks a whole string.

Color emoji are not rendered, `TYPE_AA_SDF` returns `TYPE_ERR_UNIMPLEMENTED`, and the character
width and emoji queries (`type_width()`, `type_is_emoji()` and related calls) are placeholders.

See [Type symbols](/godstack/symbols/type/) for the generated declarations and their full contracts.


<!-- END PAGE: /godstack/docs/type/ -->

<!-- BEGIN PAGE: /godstack/docs/wire/ -->
# Wire

Documentation: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/wire/
Markdown: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/docs/wire.md
Description: Handle GET requests with Wire on Unix and understand its deliberately narrow HTTP scope.


# Wire

Wire is a small blocking HTTP/1.1 server for GET requests. You supply one handler function; Wire
accepts connections, parses the request line, calls your handler, and closes the connection. It
also serves files from a `static` directory. It currently builds on Unix systems with
`sendfile()` in `<sys/sendfile.h>`, such as Linux.

Define `WIRE_IMPLEMENTATION` in exactly one translation unit before including `Wire.h`. Other
translation units include the header without it. In the implementation file, include `Wire.h`
before any system header: the implementation defines `_DEFAULT_SOURCE` to get POSIX declarations
such as `realpath()` and `sigaction()`, which only works if no system header was read first.
Alternatively, define `_DEFAULT_SOURCE` yourself at the top of that file.

## Serving a Response

The first thing to try is a server that answers every request with the same body:

```c
#define WIRE_IMPLEMENTATION
#include "Wire.h"

static int on_request(int fd, const WireHttpRequest *req, void *user)
{
    (void)req;
    (void)user;
    return wire_http_write_status(fd, 200, "text/plain", "ok\n", 3);
}

int main(void)
{
    return wire_http_serve(8080, on_request, NULL);
}
```

Run it and open `http://127.0.0.1:8080/`. `wire_http_serve()` binds `0.0.0.0:8080`, so the server
is reachable from other machines unless a firewall prevents it. On success it never returns; it
returns `-1` if the handler is NULL or the port cannot be bound. It also ignores `SIGPIPE`, so a
client that disconnects early does not kill the process.

The handler receives the connected socket, the parsed request and the `user` pointer passed to
`wire_http_serve()`. `wire_http_write_status()` writes a complete response: status line,
`Content-Type`, `Content-Length`, `Connection: close` and the body. The body may be NULL when the
length is zero. Wire closes the socket after the handler returns and ignores the return value.

## Routing Requests

`req->path` holds the request path with any query string removed (at most
`WIRE_HTTP_MAX_PATH - 1` bytes). Requests are handled one at a time, and only GET reaches the
handler: malformed requests get a `400` page and other methods a `405` page before your code
runs. Branch on the path and write one response per request:

```c
static const char home[] = "<!doctype html><title>Wire</title><h1>Hello</h1>\n";

static int route(int fd, const WireHttpRequest *req, void *user)
{
    (void)user;
    if (strcmp(req->path, "/") == 0)
        return wire_http_write_status(fd, 200, "text/html; charset=utf-8",
                                      home, sizeof home - 1);
    if (strcmp(req->path, "/health") == 0)
        return wire_http_write_status(fd, 200, "text/plain", "ok\n", 3);
    return wire_http_error(fd, 404);
}
```

`wire_http_error()` writes a small HTML page such as `<h1>404 Not Found</h1>`. The path comes from
the client: escape it before echoing it into HTML, for example with
[Cool](/godstack/docs/cool/)'s `cool_html_txt()`.

## Serving Static Files

`wire_http_serve_static()` answers `/static/...` URLs from the `static` directory under the
current working directory:

```c
if (strncmp(req->path, "/static/", 8) == 0)
    return wire_http_serve_static(fd, req->path);
```

It writes the whole response, including error pages, and returns the HTTP status it sent. The
part after `/static/` may contain only letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `-` and `/`, must not contain
`..`, and must resolve to a regular file inside `static` after symbolic links are followed.
Anything else is a `404`. The content type comes from the extension: `.html`, `.css`, `.js`,
`.svg`, `.ttf` and `.gif` are recognized, and every other file is sent as
`application/octet-stream`.

## Partial Responses for htmx

`req->hx` is nonzero when the request carries the `HX-Request: true` header that
[htmx](https://htmx.org/) sends. A handler can return just the changed fragment to htmx and a full
page to everyone else:

```c
static int counter(int fd, const WireHttpRequest *req, void *user)
{
    int *count = user;
    char body[128];
    int n;

    ++*count;
    if (req->hx)
        n = snprintf(body, sizeof body, "<span id=\"count\">%d</span>", *count);
    else
        n = snprintf(body, sizeof body,
                     "<!doctype html><button hx-get=\"/\" hx-target=\"#count\">"
                     "<span id=\"count\">%d</span></button>", *count);
    if (n < 0 || (size_t)n >= sizeof body) return wire_http_error(fd, 500);
    return wire_http_write_status(fd, 200, "text/html; charset=utf-8", body, (size_t)n);
}
```

Pass `&count` as the `user` argument of `wire_http_serve()`. Wire calls the handler from the
thread that called `wire_http_serve()`, one request at a time, so `user` state needs no locking.

## Running Your Own Loop

`wire_http_serve()` is built from four public calls. Use them directly when you need to log,
count or stop serving:

```c
int listener = wire_http_listen(8080);
if (listener < 0) return 1;

for (int served = 0; served < 100; ++served) {
    int fd = wire_http_accept(listener);
    if (fd < 0) continue;

    WireHttpRequest req;
    int status = wire_http_read_req(fd, &req);
    if (status != 0)
        wire_http_error(fd, status);
    else
        route(fd, &req, NULL);
    close(fd);
}
close(listener);
```

`wire_http_read_req()` returns `0` for a GET request, or the status to send (`400` or `405`). It
reads at most `WIRE_HTTP_MAX_REQ` bytes of request header and ignores any body. A custom loop
must ignore `SIGPIPE` itself if clients may disconnect early.

## Limits

Wire handles one connection at a time and has no timeouts, so a slow client delays everyone else.
There is no keep-alive, TLS, request body, chunked encoding or header access beyond `HX-Request`.
Put it behind a reverse proxy, or use a larger server, when you need those.

See [Wire symbols](/godstack/symbols/wire/) for the generated declarations.


<!-- END PAGE: /godstack/docs/wire/ -->

<!-- BEGIN PAGE: /godstack/guides/getting-started/ -->
# Getting Started

Documentation: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/guides/getting-started/
Markdown: https://godxgun.github.io/godstack/guides/getting-started.md
Description: Compile a minimal C99 program that embeds the Grit single-header library.


# Build a first program

Godstack libraries are single-header C libraries, simply download the raw file from the repo, clone the entire repo then copy the file 
or add the repo as a submodule; whatever you prefer. 

Once that is done, include the file directly.

## Peak - Platform Layer

Peak was the first library to be written because it's the most fundamental layer you will want to bring to almost
any program. Peak allows you to run your programs on any of the suported platforms (as of writing: Windows, Linux, MacOS 
and web). Almost no setup is required since Peak auto detects the platform at compile time and links the correct
libraries at run time.

[Main Peak Article]()

## Poof - A Build System

You don't have to use poof if you prefer other tools, but it is quite convenient.

} FuseCmd;
```

FuseCmd is the basic unit emited by fuse that your renderer will turn
into One draw record. draw() returns these packed, already in canvas space,
in emit order; z is the explicit caller layer (default 0). id is the widget
that produced the command, or 0 for anonymous geometry.

Applies to subsequently built elements. Resets to 0 on clear.

#### fuse_canvas_input_enabled {#fuse_canvas_input_enabled}

Source: `Fuse.h:277`

void       fuse_canvas_input_enabled(FuseCanvas, int enabled);
```

Gate pointer/wheel picking and captured slider updates for subsequent widgets.
Keyboard focus/edits survive; capture still ends on release. Resets on clear.
This is a builder setting, not a stack: callers restore it after a panel.

#### fuse_div_begin {#fuse_div_begin}

Source: `Fuse.h:336`

```c
void fuse_div_begin(FuseCanvas, float x, float y, float w, float h, const FuseClass *cls);
```

█                      █
█                   █
█  ███ █ █ ███ █ █ ███ █ ███ ███
█    █ █ █ █ █ █ █  █  █ █ █ █ █
